newsitem.title: USA: World Bank chief heaps praise on Mexico's Zedillo.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief heaps praise on Mexico's Zedillo.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn on Friday lavished praise on Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, saying that he had managed to bring Mexico's economic troubles under control.
Under Zedillo, Mexico has weathered one of its worst financial crises, climbing back last year after the 1995 recession caused by a massive devaluation of the peso.
"Zedillo has an excellent team. I think the issues which he's facing economically as far as I can see, are well under control," Wolfensohn told a news conference.
He acknowledged that the Mexican government faces problems outside the economic arena, but added that he had "every confidence" in Zedillo's leadership.
"I think he is a remarkable man who has grown into the job," Wolfensohn added.

A Yale-trained economist, Zedillo took office in December 1994 after winning an election as a replacement candidate of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), whose first presidential nominee was assassinated during the campaign.
Zedillo had to take drastic fiscal measures in 1995 to stabilize the economy, which contracted 6.2 percent that year.
Growth rebounded last year and Mexico posted a 5.1 percent GDP increase. In 1997, according to IMF projections, it is tipped to grow by around 4.5 percent.
The downturn, however, caused massive unemployment and a sharp fall in real wages after years of easy credit and rising consumption under predecessor Carlos Salinas de Gortari.
The PRI has paid a political price for the crisis and, for the first time in its 68 years in power, could lose its majority in Congress in July's mid-term elections.
Zedillo also faces Mexico's drug cartels, which rival Colombia's as the world's most powerful criminal groupings.
A related issue he must deal with is corruption, which surfaced earlier this year when his government had to sack its top antinarcotics official for taking bribes from a drug lord.
The World Bank is advising a group of developing countries in Latin America, Afirca and Asia on anticorruption measures.
Nevertheless, Wolfensohn said that the World Bank had not talked with Mexico directly about the problem of corruption.
"The Mexican government is a very sophisticated government, and I think they know all they need to know about how to run the country," he said.
